newsitem.title: PERU: Scant praise for Fujimori in his old neighborhood.
newsitem.headline: Scant praise for Fujimori in his old neighborhood.

text.p: World leaders envy him for his gritty resolve and his own troops call him a hero, but back in his old neighbourhood not everyone thinks so highly of Peru's President Alberto Fujimori.

People in Lima's hardscrabble district of La Victoria are harsh in their judgments about their most famous son, as he basks in praise for rescuing 71 out of 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's house this week.
"Fujimori did it to revive his popularity, isn't that obvious? But around here, there's no work and not much hope," said Moises Huanca, standing outside his bankrupt trucking company in La Victoria.

On Avenida Grau, the bustling avenue where Fujimori spent his early childhood, residents say he occasionally breezes through on his way to inaugurate a school or some other function. But that is about all they see of him.

And while many are grateful to him for wiping out Peru's two leftist guerrilla insurgencies, the Shining Path and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), crime, unemployment and poverty are what people really care about.

"Maybe Fujimori spent his childhood here, but that sure hasn't benefited us at all," said Rafael Valera, 40, as he walked with his daughter down Lucanas street in the heart of the district of crumbling old homes and working-class families.

"It's true there is no more terrorism, but there is no work, either. It's like we had to exchange one problem for the other," said Valera, who has lived in the area for 18 years but still calls himself a newcomer.
Women seem to admire the president's resolve in unusually large numbers.

"Fujimori did everything he could for the terrorists. He even let them go to Cuba. But let's face it, they wanted blood, and he gave it to them. I think he did the right thing," said Lupe Alvarez, selling cake at her tiny stand on Avenida Grau.

Fujimori's Japanese immigrant father ran a tire shop in the neighbourhood. The area still has many tire and automotive stores, but the hard-striving Asian immigrants who once predominated have now moved on to more respectable districts.
"His family lived around here but as soon as (Fujimori) got his engineering degree, he went off to live in San Isidro," a rich suburb, said long-time resident Arturo Sanchez.
No one can remember when Peru was anything but poor, but Fujimori takes most of the blame anyway as residents speak with resignation and flashes of anger of everyday hardships.

"My whole family has to dedicate itself to street hawking because there is no other work," said Linda Vera as she cooked up stew and rice for customers at a rickety lunch stand. "Where I live everyone is poor and we have water for only about an hour every three days. It's hard on the kids."
Though everyone praises him for winning the liberation of the hostages, they also fault Fujimori for not sparing the lives of the 14 MRTA hostage-takers.
"Why couldn't he bring them out with their hands up? Then you could call it a success. But no, they had to bomb the place with no respect for human life," said doctor Walter Abad.
"They were all kids, 15 years old some of them. But they killed them anyway," said his assistant, Juan Chavez.
They cited the capture of Shining Path leader Abimael Guzman as an example of what Fujimori should have done with the MRTA guerrillas -- arrest them, try them and put them away for life.

"They made peace with Ecuador, why can't we make peace with the MRTA? The whole time the government was negotiating, it was building those tunnels and planning to kill them all," said tire shop employee Carlos Rodriguez. He was referring to Peru's peace talks with Ecuador to settle a border dispute.

But others were not so critical. "The only people who criticise Fujimori are the leftists. But don't forget what it was like when he took over (in 1990). We lived in total chaos and misery," said one man who declined to give his name.
Despite the triumph over guerrillas, people are dour and pessimistic about the future.

"If you don't have a job, nothing goes right," said Valera. "You get sick and you can't afford to go to the doctor. And that's what's happening to Peru -- we're a country that doesn't have a job so we don't get better."
